title: Aerospace and Automotive Safety: Where They Agree and Differ
summary: Both domains use disciplined, evidence-based engineering to reduce safety risk. They differ mainly in risk classification, approval context, operational assumptions, standards structure and the assurance burden placed on software and certification evidence.
caution: This comparison uses approximate conceptual mappings for learning. ASIL and DAL/software levels are not interchangeable, HARA is not the same as FHA, and an ISO 26262 safety argument is not a DO-178C certification package.

sharedPrinciples.title: Safety starts above software
sharedPrinciples.summary: Both domains begin from vehicle, aircraft or system behaviour and allocate requirements downward. Software is one implementation element within a wider safety argument.

sharedPrinciples.title: Risk determines rigour
sharedPrinciples.summary: The required depth of development and verification depends on the consequence of failure, although each domain classifies that risk differently.

sharedPrinciples.title: Requirements and traceability matter
sharedPrinciples.summary: High-level intent must be decomposed, reviewed, traced and verified through architecture, design, implementation and test evidence.

sharedPrinciples.title: Architecture is part of the assurance argument
sharedPrinciples.summary: Independence, partitioning, redundancy, monitoring, fault containment and interface control are used to prevent one fault or error from defeating the intended safety behaviour.

sharedPrinciples.title: Verification must be planned and objective
sharedPrinciples.summary: Reviews, analysis, testing, coverage and independence are planned lifecycle activities rather than late quality checks.

sharedPrinciples.title: Configuration and change control are essential
sharedPrinciples.summary: A claim is meaningful only when the exact requirements, code, models, tools, tests, reports and approved baselines can be identified and reproduced.

sharedPrinciples.title: Evidence is part of the product
sharedPrinciples.summary: Plans, analyses, traceability, review records, test results, coverage data, problem reports and approval records are deliverables, not administrative leftovers.

sharedPrinciples.title: Changes require impact analysis
sharedPrinciples.summary: A small code change can reopen requirements, architecture, safety analysis, verification, configuration and approval activities in both domains.

differences.automotive: ISO 26262 is commonly applied through OEM, supplier, assessor and organisational safety processes to demonstrate that the applicable functional-safety lifecycle has been fulfilled.
differences.aerospace: DO-178C software evidence supports compliance within an aircraft, engine, equipment or TSO certification programme reviewed through certification-authority or authorised-representative processes.
differences.practicalEffect: Aerospace teams prepare objective certification evidence and authority-facing review readiness from the beginning; automotive teams prepare lifecycle evidence for product, organisational and assessment decisions.

differences.automotive: HARA assigns QM or ASIL A-D using severity, exposure and controllability for hazardous events in road-vehicle operating situations.
differences.aerospace: Aircraft and system failure conditions are classified by aircraft-level effects; development-assurance and software levels are allocated through system development and safety-assessment processes.
differences.practicalEffect: ASIL D is not equivalent to DAL A. The inputs, assumptions, objectives and approval consequences differ even when both indicate high criticality.

differences.automotive: Driver or road-user controllability is an explicit HARA input and can influence the assigned ASIL.
differences.aerospace: Crew response, annunciation, workload, flight phase and operational procedures are considered within aircraft-level failure-condition assessment rather than an automotive S-E-C formula.
differences.practicalEffect: A mitigation that relies on a trained crew, dispatch limitation or operating procedure cannot be translated directly into a driver-controllability argument.

differences.automotive: ISO 26262 is an integrated series covering management, concept, system, hardware, software, production, supporting processes and safety analyses.
differences.aerospace: Aircraft and system development, safety assessment, software, airborne electronic hardware, tool qualification, model-based development and related assurance topics are distributed across coordinated standards such as ARP4754B, ARP4761A, DO-178C, DO-254, DO-330 and DO-331.
differences.practicalEffect: Aerospace assurance boundaries must be coordinated across several standards and approval plans; automotive teams work within one broader functional-safety series plus complementary standards.

differences.automotive: ISO 26262-6 places software inside the complete E/E functional-safety lifecycle and connects it to safety requirements, architecture, hardware metrics, safety mechanisms and vehicle-level validation.
differences.aerospace: DO-178C is specifically focused on airborne software lifecycle objectives and certification evidence, with supplements for model-based development, object-oriented technology, formal methods and tools.
differences.practicalEffect: Aerospace typically demands more explicit objective-by-objective software evidence; automotive places comparatively greater emphasis on the complete E/E safety architecture and vehicle-level risk reduction.

differences.automotive: Coverage methods are selected as part of software verification according to ASIL, method recommendations and project strategy.
differences.aerospace: Structural coverage analysis is closely tied to software level and is used to identify missing requirements-based tests, unintended functionality, deactivated code and source-to-object concerns where applicable.
differences.practicalEffect: A statement such as '100% coverage' is insufficient by itself in either domain and does not establish DO-178C compliance without the required requirements-based and structural analysis context.

differences.automotive: ISO 26262 explicitly addresses systematic failures and random hardware failures, including hardware architectural metrics, probabilistic evaluation, dependent failures and safety analyses.
differences.aerospace: Aircraft and system safety assessments use qualitative and quantitative analyses under ARP4761A, while software development assurance primarily addresses systematic development errors rather than assigning software a random failure rate like a physical component.
differences.practicalEffect: The software assurance case must be connected to system architecture and hardware safety, but the analytical treatment and allocation mechanisms differ.

differences.automotive: Very high production volume, platform reuse, cost pressure, supplier chains, vehicle variants, uncontrolled road environments and OTA updates strongly influence the safety process.
differences.aerospace: Lower production volume, long certified service life, tightly controlled configurations, trained crews, dispatch rules, maintenance organisations and formal modification approval shape the assurance process.
differences.practicalEffect: Automotive emphasises scalable lifecycle execution and variant management; aerospace emphasises controlled approved baselines, certification records and modification discipline.

mappings.aerospace: Aircraft/system function definition and operational context
mappings.note: Both establish scope and boundaries, but the artefacts, hierarchy and certification context differ.
Both identify hazardous outcomes, but HARA uses severity, exposure and controllability while FHA classifies failure conditions by aircraft-level effect.

mappings.aerospace: Failure condition in an operational context
mappings.note: The concepts are useful analogies, not interchangeable terms.

mappings.aerospace: Aircraft/system safety objective or allocated safety requirement
mappings.note: Both express required safety outcomes, but allocation and approval flows differ.
No one-to-one conversion exists. Do not equate ASIL D with DAL A.

mappings.aerospace: Functional architecture, implementation architecture and allocated safety requirements
mappings.note: Both connect safety intent to architecture, but the lifecycle artefacts and terminology are different.

mappings.automotive: Safety mechanisms and freedom from interference
mappings.aerospace: Monitoring, redundancy, partitioning, independence and fault containment
mappings.note: The engineering patterns may look similar while their assurance objectives and credit differ.

mappings.aerospace: Independent lifecycle reviews, quality assurance, certification reviews and compliance findings
mappings.note: Both use independent evidence review, but authority involvement and approval consequences are different.
Both require controlled evidence and residual-risk decisions; aerospace approval is embedded in the certification context.

automotive.title: Automotive engine controller
automotive.hazardContext: A representative hazardous event is unintended engine torque at a defined vehicle speed and road-operating situation.
automotive.assessment: The team evaluates severity, exposure and driver controllability, assigns an ASIL, creates safety goals and allocates system, hardware and software safety requirements.
automotive.assuranceFocus: The implementation may use torque arbitration, monitoring, diagnostics and degraded operation, supported by ISO 26262 lifecycle evidence and vehicle-level validation.

aerospace.title: Aircraft engine controller
aerospace.hazardContext: Representative failure conditions include loss of commanded thrust, erroneous high thrust, uncommanded shutdown, misleading indication or combined propulsion effects at aircraft level.
aerospace.assessment: Aircraft and engine safety processes assess the operational effects, crew response, remaining capability and architecture, then allocate development-assurance and software levels.
aerospace.assuranceFocus: The software fulfils the applicable DO-178C lifecycle objectives and produces certification evidence for the controlled approved configuration, including requirements, design, code, target verification, coverage and problem closure.

engineControlExample.lesson: The control algorithms, models, target processors and buses may look technically familiar. The risk argument, lifecycle allocation, authority interaction and approval evidence are not the same.

references.title: AC 20-115D — Airborne Software Development Assurance Using ED-12( ) and DO-178( )
references.note: Active FAA advisory circular recognising DO-178C and related supplements as an acceptable means of compliance for airborne software.

references.title: ARP4754B — Guidelines for Development of Civil Aircraft and Systems
references.note: Aircraft and system development guidance that refers detailed software assurance to DO-178C and safety assessment to ARP4761A.

references.title: ARP4761A — Guidelines for Conducting the Safety Assessment Process
references.note: Civil-aircraft, system and equipment safety-assessment guidance, including failure-condition and architecture assessment processes.

references.title: ISO 26262 road vehicles functional safety package
references.note: Official overview of the ISO 26262:2018 series covering management, concept, system, hardware, software, production, supporting processes and safety analyses.

references.title: ISO 26262-3:2018 — Concept phase
references.note: Official ISO overview of item definition, hazard analysis and risk assessment, and the functional safety concept.
